note: Batch 7 (2026-11-23 sleep work): water and ice, from weather.gov (US federal) and the Minnesota DNR (official state agency, dnr.state.mn.us). Draft: not reviewed by experts.

guides.title: Caught in a rip current
guides.summary: Being pulled out to sea by a current at the beach.

steps.text: Stay calm. A rip current pulls you out, not under.
steps.quote: Rip currents don't pull you under

steps.text: Don't swim straight back to shore against it. It can be faster than an Olympic swimmer and will wear you out.
steps.quote: Trying to swim against a rip current will only use up your energy

steps.text: Swim along the shoreline until you're out of the pull, then swim at an angle back toward shore.
steps.quote: Swim along the shoreline until you escape the current's pull

steps.text: If you can't make it, float, face the shore, and call or wave for help.
steps.quote: If you feel you can't reach shore, relax, face the shore, and call or wave for help

guides.title: Fell through ice
guides.summary: You (or someone) broke through ice into the water.

steps.text: Try not to panic. Keep your winter clothes on: they trap air and help you float.
steps.quote: Heavy clothes won't drag you down, but instead can trap air to provide warmth and flotation

steps.text: Turn back toward the way you came. That ice is probably the strongest.
steps.quote: Turn toward the direction you came

steps.text: Put your hands and arms on the unbroken ice. Kick your feet and pull yourself forward onto it. Ice picks, nails or keys help you grip.
steps.quote: Kick your feet and dig in your ice picks to work your way back onto the solid ice

steps.text: Once you're out, stay flat and roll away from the hole to spread your weight.
steps.quote: Lie flat on the ice once you are out and roll away from the hole

steps.text: Get somewhere warm, dry and sheltered and warm up right away. Get medical help if you're badly chilled.
steps.quote: Get to a warm, dry, sheltered area and re-warm yourself immediately

guides.title: Someone is in the water
guides.summary: Someone has fallen through ice, or is struggling in the water, and you want to help.

steps.text: Call for help first. Don't run to the edge: you could end up in the water too.
steps.quote: Resist the urge to run up to the edge of the hole

steps.text: Shout to them that help is coming, and keep encouraging them.
steps.quote: Shout to the victim to encourage them to fight to survive

steps.text: Reach: from a safe spot, hold out a rope, branch, ladder or jumper cables. If they start pulling you in, let go and try again.
steps.quote: If the person starts to pull you in, release your grip on the object and start over

steps.text: Throw: toss them a rope or something that floats. If it's a rope, have them tie it around themselves before the cold weakens their grip.
steps.quote: Toss one end of a rope or something that will float to the victim

steps.text: Don't go out to them yourself unless nothing else is possible. Untrained rescuers often drown too.
steps.quote: A non-professional shouldn't go out on the ice to perform a rescue unless all other basic rescue techniques have been ruled out

steps.text: Cold water makes people gasp and breathe fast, so a fall into cold water can drown even strong swimmers. A life jacket buys time.
steps.quote: The sudden gasp and rapid breathing alone creates a greater risk of drowning, even for confident swimmers in calm waters
